introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá left no treatise on education, but his letters and table talk about schools are specific. Teach by conversation and by questions; let children discuss a spiritual topic each day; keep lessons within six hours; let each child follow the bent of his talent; teach a universal language; join moral education to science, since a school that trains the mind alone produces clever people without character. Socrates’s midwifery and the boy asking questions in the temple are the method; Plato and Aristotle on forming character, Milton on the end of learning and Bacon on reading are the tradition; Locke’s blank paper is the modern starting point that the readings supplement.
questions: Why teach by question and answer? What does it do that a lecture cannot?
Reading 5 lets the child’s inclination choose the subject. What are the limits of that principle?
What do the readings think is lacking in a purely “material” education? Is it something a school can supply?

outside.why: Most ideas taught through speech; one child questions another. Socrates called his teaching midwifery: I look after their souls when they are in labour.
Teaching by question and answer. They found him in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions.
No more than six hours a day. Much study is a weariness of the flesh.
One divine topic each day for the children to discuss. Thou shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way.
If a child has a liking for commerce, let him choose commerce. Train up a child in the way he should go.
Once they are skilled readers. Bacon: reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
Schools that teach only material subjects. Milton: the end of learning is to repair the ruins of our first parents by regaining to know God aright.

Locke began from the other end: the mind is white paper, void of all characters, and all its materials come from experience. Does an education that starts from experience have room for what reading 7 says is missing?
Three cardinal principles for universities. Aristotle: music has a power of forming the character, and should therefore be introduced into the education of the young.
The goal is a citizen of the Kingdom of God. The beginning is the most important part, for that is the time at which the character is being formed.
A universal language taught in all schools. The whole earth was of one language, and of one speech.
Whatever is undertaken should be carried out with perfection. Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might.
Teachers must both educate and teach. Confucius: learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.

shortfall: Readings 11 and 14 to 19 concern particular schools and plans, for which no companion from outside was sought.
